persona.name: Birgit (née Sundqvist)
persona.born: 1935, Sollefteå, Ångermanland (river and timber town, regiment I 21)
persona.family: Father a sawmill worker and log-floater, mother at home, Mission Covenant chapel on Sundays. Married Gösta (b. 1933, Göinge, northern Skåne; fitter who came north for the power-station construction on the Ångerman river) in 1958. Children born 1959, 1962, 1965.
persona.emigration: 1971 to Prince George, British Columbia, where Gösta took a millwright job at a pulp mill. Stayed; widowed later, still in BC in 2026 aged 91.
persona.howMusicReachedHer: 1935-49: parents' wind-up gramophone (Jularbo accordion), chapel hymns, school songs, the single Radiotjänst channel (Barnens brevlåda, Grammofontimmen, Frukostklubben from 1946). 1950-59: Karusellen with Lennart Hyland, Saturday dances at the Folkets park and logdans, cinema, a few 78s then EPs; TV reached us about 1959-60 (exact year unsure). 1960-71: kitchen radio all day, Melodiradion from 1961, Svensktoppen from 1962, Hylands hörna and Melodifestivalen on TV, Sven-Ingvars at the folkpark. 1971-95 in BC: CKPG AM radio in the kitchen, CBC television (Tommy Hunter Show, Irish Rovers, Juno broadcasts), country radio in the car, the children's records through the wall; and at home the crate of Swedish LPs, cassettes sent by my sister, Swedish Christmas and Midsummer gatherings, a visit home every few years.
persona.unsure: Release years marked unsure above; exact arrival of TV in Sollefteå; several Thory Bernhards / Lily Berglund / Lasse Lönndahl seed titles I cannot date with confidence and marked 'maybe'.

gp1.wouldSay: I was in the cradle. Taube and Rolf I know, but from later, from everybody singing them. The American jazz was not in our kitchen in Sollefteå; Pappa's gramophone had Jularbo and Mamma sang hymns.

gp1.fake: Four of six seeds are American swing/jazz for a Stockholm restaurant crowd; in a Norrland small town in the 30s it was accordion, schlager on the one radio channel, hymns and children's songs (Alice Tegnér). Both Swedish seeds predate the stop (1931, 1920s). Nobody 'remembers' age 0-4; this stop can only be the parents' music.

gp2.wouldSay: Min soldat, yes, that is the war, Pappa away on beredskap and Ulla Billquist on the radio. Swing it magistern we sang in the schoolyard. But Zarah in German and Karl Gerhard's horse, that was not for a child in Ångermanland.

gp2.fake: Zarah Leander in German: Swedes knew her Swedish records, the UFA originals were not Swedish radio fare. White Christmas reached Sweden after the war, not 1942-44. Trojan horse is a history-book song, a Stockholm revue number that was banned, not something a child heard. No children's radio (Barnens brevlåda), no accordion, no school songs.

gp3.wouldSay: This is the same list as before! Räkna de lyckliga, Johansson, Zarah, White Christmas again. And Zarah was not played in Sweden after the war, she was frozen out. Where is Frukostklubben, where is Bertil Boo, Yngve Stoor at Christmas?

Zarah Leander 1945-49 is historically wrong: she was persona non grata in Sweden until about 1949. Nothing in the list sounds like peace arriving.

gp4.wouldSay: Now it is me. Snoddas in Karusellen, we all sat at the radio that Saturday, and Flottarkärlek is our river. Lasse Lönndahl, yes, I had his picture. Vildandens sång, Valpen i fönstret. But four Thory and four Lasse, and Zarah in German again?

Zarah Leander - Wunderbar in German does not belong. No dance music: at 17-19 I was at the Folkets park and the logdans every Saturday, and none of that is here.

gp5.wouldSay: Rock Around the Clock at the cinema, Little Gerhard, Martin Ljung's Rock-Fnykis made us cry laughing. Kärleksbrev i sanden was when Gösta and I were courting, Vita syrener at our wedding dance. Augustin on the new television.

gp8.wouldSay: Pippi was the children's, they sang it in the car to Gothenburg. Anna och mej, My Sweet Lord on the radio while we packed. But this is six songs for the biggest year of my life, and not one of them is about leaving.

gp10.wouldSay: You Needed Me, You Light Up My Life, The Homecoming from the tea advertisement, the Edmund Fitzgerald. Night Fever was our daughter's. Gens du pays I have never heard in my life. And ABBA was on Canadian radio every hour and is not here.

Céline is represented by a French song when in BC she was the English ballads. Grunge and Britpop for a grandmother.

journey.order: Order is right, lengths are not. Five-year slices are calendar, not life. 1935-39 (age 0-4) cannot stand as a stop: merge 1935-44 into one 'childhood, parents' music' stop where older songs are allowed. 1940-44 and 1945-49 come out as nearly the same list, so either merge them or force them apart (war vs peace). 1950-64 is the heart (ages 15-29) and works. 1970-71 is too short and thin as an ordinary stop; it should be 'the leaving'. The Canadian side is five stops of declining relevance, 6-6-3-3-4, and it ends in 1995 when I was 60: thirty years of my life in BC (retirement, grandchildren, Gösta's last years, Swedish radio and Allsång på Skansen over the internet) are simply absent.
journey.transitions: The emigration is not felt at all: one stop is 100% Sweden, the next is 100% Canadian chart, as if I had been swapped for a Canadian born there. In reality the house stayed Swedish for a decade: the LPs we brought, tapes from home, Lucia and Midsummer with the other Scandinavians, and enormous pride when ABBA, Blue Swede, later Roxette and Ace of Base came on Canadian radio. None of that thread exists; ABBA is not seeded once in 24 Canadian years. No leaving songs at 1970-71 (Hälsa dem därhemma, Barndomshemmet, Är det konstigt att man längtar bort nån gång). No return visits (we went home in 1977 and 1986 and came back with the records of that summer). The Canadian prompts literally ask for 'the way someone who grew up there remembers it', which is the wrong instruction for an immigrant who arrived at 36.
journey.repeats: Yes. gp2 and gp3 share four seeds (Räkna de lyckliga stunderna blott, Johanssons boogie-woogie-vals, Zarah Leander's Ich weiß..., White Christmas), which makes 1945-49 a rerun of the war. The Zarah repeat is the worst: it is placed in exactly the years she was shut out of Sweden. Hélène repeats in gp12 and gp13 and I never knew it either time. Within stops, one artist is repeated too much: Thory Bernhards x4, Lasse Lönndahl x4, Lily Berglund x4 in gp4; Anne Murray x3 in gp10; Glass Tiger x2 and Corey Hart x2 in gp12.
journey.change: After the move, stop generating 'Canada as a native remembers it' and generate 'what a Swedish immigrant woman of my age in British Columbia heard': the English-Canadian adult radio and CBC television for her age and region (no Quebec French chart, no teen rock), plus a continuing Swedish thread at home (records brought along, new Swedish hits arriving by tape and visit, Swedish acts on Canadian radio). That one change fixes the transition, the falling scores of gp9-gp13, and the Quebec problem together.
journey.notes: Seeds track the national chart, which coincides with my taste only between about 15 and 35; before that I was a child hearing my parents' music, after 40 the chart belongs to my children. Scores follow that exactly: 3,6,4 / 8,8,9,8 / 6 / 6,6,3,3,4. Canadian seeds count Quebec francophone hits as 'local' (11 French songs across gp9-gp13); for BC they are foreign. Anachronisms: Great Big Sea 1997 in a 1990-95 stop; Zarah Leander in 1945-49; White Christmas in 1940-44 Sweden. Gösta (b. 1933, Göinge in Skåne) would differ: he grew up with Edvard Persson films and Danish radio in reach, so he would ask for Edvard Persson in gp1-gp3 and care less for the Norrland colour (Flottarkärlek is my river, not his); Göingeflickorna's Kära mor and Thore Skogman's Älgjakten are his songs more than mine. Two years older, he was a swing-mad teenager in 1946-49 and would say yes to Rum and Coca-Cola, Glenn Miller and want Thore Ehrling and Alice Babs, so gp3 might be a 5 for him. He never cared for Lasse Lönndahl; gp4 would be a 6. In Canada he heard the lunchroom and truck radio at the mill, country and rock: he knows BTO, April Wine, Loverboy by ear and would miss Stompin' Tom Connors, Charley Pride and Johnny Cash, and Hockey Night in Canada's theme; he would give gp9-gp11 a point more than I do, but he would miss the Swedish thread just as much, especially accordion and Taube. Unsure items are flagged in the missing lists and persona.
